decision: Build a tool that checks whether an AI-written fix is actually tested

opportunity.subject: reviewing changes an agent wrote, for developers who already drown in them
opportunity.notes: Not a business. An open-source tool, scored on the same scale as everything else here, because the screen asks where to point effort and not whether money changes hands.

cost_detached.evidence: A reviewer reads thirty reports to find one real defect. That ratio is set by nobody having automated the check, not by anything intrinsic to reviewing.

absorbable.evidence: The expensive part is running a new test against the old code, and that is precisely what a command-line tool with git and a shell can do itself.

soft_barrier.evidence: Mostly convention — but mutation testing is adjacent, has existed for years, and stayed niche because it is slow and noisy. That is a real reason, not just habit, so this is not a 2.

existing_need.evidence: The pain exists today, in the author's own week, which is the only demand signal worth much at this stage.

pulls_help.evidence: 'Red before green, or it didn't happen' is a line people repeat. It is still a developer tool, not a cause, and scoring it higher would be scoring the wish.

reachable_proof.evidence: A working prototype is a weekend. Nothing here needs anyone's permission or money.

requirements.text: Must support Python, Go and TypeScript at launch
Must never send repository contents to a third party without consent
Should offer at most three candidate tests per change

steps.name: Infer what the change claims to fix
Generate candidate tests that would fail if the claim were false
Run each candidate against the base commit and keep only the red ones
Render a syntax-highlighted diff in the report

components.name: One agent-written change, reviewed by hand
